Drought has touched this county in 19 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025, with 2024 the worst year at 19 weeks. No solar or wind capacity operates here, and none is proposed to EIA.

54107.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Wood County runs $55 per acre in 2026, up 64.2 percent from 2016. Land sold for $4,290 per acre in the 2022 census, with values up 28.7 percent from 2017 to 2022, 5.2 percent a year. July nights average 65.1 F for 2017-2026 against a 63.5 F normal for 1991-2020, part of a warming trend of 0.5 F per decade since 1976. Drought has touched the county in 22 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025, with 2024 the worst year at 18 weeks. No solar or wind capacity operates or is proposed here.

54109.text: Land here is valued at $3,991 per acre by operators, up 19.2 percent from 2017-2022, or 3.6 percent a year. July nights average 63 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 62 F, with a warming trend of 0.42 F per decade since 1976; no July since 1900 has averaged 70 F or above. Drought has touched this county in 30 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025, 2.2 percent of the time, with 2007 the worst year at 10 weeks, and 6 weeks from 2021-2025. No solar or wind capacity operates here, and none is proposed to EIA.

56001.text: Land in Albany County carries a census value of $1,040 per acre, up 42.3 percent from 2017-2022, 7.3 percent a year. Irrigation covers 81 percent of harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from groundwater as of 2015. Drought has touched the county in 238 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025, 17.5 percent of the record, with 2002 the worst year at 46 weeks; from 2021-2025 the count is 51 weeks. The July nightly low averaged 49.9 F from 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 49 F, with a warming trend of 0.5 F per decade since 1976. Wind capacity in the county stands at 487.1 MW operating, with 504 MW more proposed to EIA.

56003.text: Irrigated cash rent here runs $106 per acre, against $23 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and 82 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Groundwater supplies only 1 percent of that irrigation, so this county depends on surface water. Heat and drought's share of crop insurance indemnities has moved from 3 percent in 1989-1999 to 9 percent in 2000-2009, 7 percent in 2010-2019, and 23 percent in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost remains the largest cause of indemnities overall, at 33 percent.

56005.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in 2019 averaged $10 per acre. Land value came in at $959 per acre in 2022, up 69.4 percent, 11.1 percent a year, from 2017. Heat and drought drove 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and that cause's share rose in each period listed: 19 percent in 1989-1999, 53 percent in 2000-2009, 67 percent in 2010-2019, 81 percent in 2020-2025. The county spent 384 of 1357 weeks, 28.3 percent, in severe drought or worse from 2000-2025, with 99 of those weeks falling in 2021-2025. July nightly lows have warmed 0.54 F per decade since 1976, and cropland irrigation covers 7 percent of harvested acres.

56007.text: Irrigated cash rent in Carbon County runs $24 per acre, against $971 per acre for land and buildings in the 2022 census. Irrigation covers 96 percent of harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from groundwater as of 2015. Land value rose 76.5 percent from 2017-2022, 12 percent a year. Drought has touched the county in 327 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025, with 2003 the worst year at 52 weeks; 2021-2025 saw 31 such weeks. July nightly lows have warmed 0.4 F per decade since 1976, and the 2017-2026 average of 51.6 F sits above the 1991-2020 normal of 50.6 F. Wind operations already total 1754.6 MW, with 3556.6 MW more proposed.

56009.text: Irrigated cash rent in 2021 runs $50 per acre, against $12 per acre for non-irrigated land in 2020, and 76 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated as of the 2022 census. Groundwater supplied only 2 percent of irrigation water in 2015, so this land depends on surface supply. Heat and drought made up 1 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, then 53 percent in 2010-2019, then 56 percent in 2020-2025. The county spent 73 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025, out of 381 such weeks counted from 2000-2025. July nightly lows have warmed 0.4 F per decade since 1976, and the 2017-2026 average of 55.1 F sits above the 1991-2020 normal of 54.2 F.

56011.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Crook County runs $14 per acre. Heat and drought account for 68 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and the share has moved through 26 percent in 1989-1999, 62 percent in 2000-2009, 71 percent in 2010-2019, and 80 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.93, and for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 it is 1.05. July nightly lows average 56.4 F over 2017-2026, up from a 1991-2020 normal of 55.1 F, with a warming trend of 0.54 F per decade since 1976.

56013.text: Irrigated land dominates here: 94 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $78 per acre against $15 per acre non-irrigated. July nights have warmed 0.46 F per decade since 1976, and the 2017-2026 average of 51.1 F sits above the 1991-2020 normal of 50 F. Weeks in severe drought or worse ran 379 of 1357 from 2000-2025, with 50 of those weeks falling in 2021-2025.

56015.text: Irrigation covers 66 percent of harvested cropland, with 24 percent of that water drawn from groundwater in 2015. Land value hit $1,871 per acre in 2022, up 117.1 percent from 2017. Drought held 32.9 percent of weeks at severe or worse from 2000-2025, with 135 weeks in 2021-2025 alone.

56017.text: Every acre of harvested cropland in Hot Springs County is irrigated, and only 3 percent of that irrigation water comes from groundwater, 2015. Irrigation failure is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities, 1997-2022, at 71 percent, totaling $167,408 of $237,346 in closed-year claims. Heat and drought made up 0 percent of indemnities 2000-2009 and 4 percent 2010-2019. The county spent 75 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025, against 421 of 1357 weeks over 2000-2025, with 2002 the worst year at 53 weeks. July nightly lows have warmed 0.57 F per decade since 1976, and land value rose 32.5 percent from 2017-2022.

56019.text: Irrigated cropland here rents for $78 per acre in 2026; non-irrigated cash rent averages $9 per acre in 2024. Eighty percent of harvested cropland was irrigated as of the 2022 census, and none of that water came from groundwater in 2015. Drought has been a recurring feature: the county spent 404 of 1357 weeks at severe drought or worse from 2000-2025, with 97 such weeks in 2021-2025 alone, and 2002 logged 53 weeks. Crop insurance paid out $4.4 million over 1989-2021, mostly through area and index plans with no peril assigned at 90 percent; heat and drought made up 2 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, and irrigation failure claims totaled $140,169. The loss ratio across 1989-2025 stands at 1.84.

56021.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Laramie County is $28 per acre for 2026, up 37.5 percent from 2016. Irrigated rent runs $112 per acre in 2025, and irrigation covers 25 percent of harvested cropland, with 71 percent of that water drawn from groundwater as of 2015. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, at 36 percent of $74.3 million paid, and its share has moved unevenly across periods: 5 percent in 1989-1999, 33 percent in 2000-2009, 27 percent in 2010-2019, and 52 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low averaged 54.7 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.6 F, warming at 0.49 F per decade since 1976. Census land value sits at $2,003 per acre for 2022, up 136.2 percent from 2017.

56023.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Lincoln County is $30 per acre in 2026, up 62.2 percent from 2016. Eighty-one percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of that water is not from groundwater, at 2 percent in 2015. Drought weeks ran 400 of 1357 from 2000-2025, with 113 of those weeks falling in 2021-2025 alone. July nights have warmed since 1976 at 0.47 F per decade, and the 2017-2026 average low, 46.7 F, sits above the 1991-2020 normal of 45.3 F. Land value rose 116.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, reaching $3,963 per acre.

56025.text: Irrigated cash rent in Natrona County is $89 per acre, against a non-irrigated rate of $12 per acre in 2012. Irrigation covers 93 percent of harvested cropland, and all of it comes from surface water, with 0 percent from groundwater in 2015. Crop insurance indemnities since 1990 total $2.1 million, with heat and drought the largest cause at 40 percent overall; that share was 76 percent in 1989-1999, 70 percent in 2000-2009, 14 percent in 2010-2019, and 6 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks ran 377 of 1357 from 2000-2025, with 43 from 2021-2025. Wind operations stand at 141.3 MW; solar is 0 MW.

56027.text: Irrigated cropland here rents for $135 per acre in 2026, against $14 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and irrigation draws 91 percent of its water from groundwater as of 2015. Non-irrigated rent is up 16.7 percent from 2013 to 2025. The heat and drought share of crop insurance indemnities has moved 3 percent, 9 percent, 48 percent, 55 percent across 1989-1999, 2000-2009, 2010-2019, and 2020-2025. July nightly lows have warmed 0.54 F per decade since 1976, and the 2017-2026 average of 57.5 F sits above the 1991-2020 normal of 56.2 F. Census land value rose 26.2 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 4.8 percent a year.

56029.text: Irrigated cropland in Park County rents for $110 per acre in 2026, against $30 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2021. Irrigation covers 89 percent of harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from groundwater. July nights have warmed from 46.6 F normal to 47.8 F in 2017-2026, a trend of 0.56 F per decade. Land values rose 90.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

56031.text: Cash rent in Platte County runs $22 per acre non-irrigated and $120 per acre irrigated, with 60 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation as of the 2022 census. Groundwater supplies 17 percent of that irrigation water, so most of it comes from surface sources. Heat and drought's share of crop insurance indemnities has moved 1 percent, 20 percent, 24 percent, 32 percent across 1989-1999, 2000-2009, 2010-2019, and 2020-2025. Hail remains the largest single cause of indemnities over 1989-2025 at 26 percent, and irrigation failure alone has cost $5.7 million across all closed years. Land value rose 17.1 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 3.2 percent a year.

56033.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Sheridan County runs $20 per acre, and irrigated land leases at $50 per acre. Land value and buildings were estimated at $1,582 per acre in 2022, up 29.2 percent from 2017, 5.3 percent a year. Irrigated cropland covers 55 percent of harvested acres, and none of that water comes from groundwater. The July nightly low has warmed 0.62 F per decade since 1976, and the heat and drought share of crop insurance indemnities climbed across each listed period: 19 percent in 1989-1999, 32 percent in 2000-2009, 40 percent in 2010-2019, 81 percent in 2020-2025.

56035.text: Irrigated cash rent in Sublette County was $30 per acre in 2025, and non-irrigated cash rent was $21 per acre in 2023, up 40 percent from 2013. Share of harvested cropland irrigated was 97 percent in 2022, with 11 percent of irrigation water from groundwater in 2015. Land value stood at $2,038 per acre in 2022, up 23.4 percent from 2017, or 4.3 percent a year. Drought was present here: 440 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025 saw severe drought or worse, with 2002 the worst year at 53 weeks, and 110 such weeks fell in 2021-2025.

56037.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Sweetwater County runs $32 per acre, irrigated $44 per acre. Cropland here leans on water: 92 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, though only 11 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. Drought has been a recurring feature, with 404 of 1357 weeks at 50 percent of the county or worse in severe drought or worse from 2000-2025, and 2003 alone carried 52 weeks. The July nightly low has moved from a 1991-2020 normal of 50.9 F to 52.3 F over 2017-2026, part of a warming trend of 0.59 F per decade since 1976. Land value rose 30.7 percent from 2017-2022.

56039.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Teton County stands at $40 per acre in 2026, up 158.1 percent from 2016. Irrigated cash rent runs slightly higher, at $45 per acre. Irrigated cropland covers 67 percent of harvested acres, all of it drawn from surface water, with none from groundwater in 2015. Drought has touched the county in 375 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025, with 131 of those weeks falling in 2021-2025.

56045.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Weston County averaged $17 per acre in 2023, up 25.9 percent from 2012. Land value came in at $953 per acre in 2022, up 42.5 percent from 2017, or 7.3 percent a year. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities across 1989-2025, at 43 percent of $7.0 million paid, and its share rose from 29 percent in 2000-2009 to 74 percent in 2010-2019 and stood at 67 percent in 2020-2025. The county spent 84 weeks in severe drought or worse during 2021-2025, against 353 of 1357 weeks over 2000-2025.
